We observe that patients typically struggle to blink on the affected side, creating a distinct contrast in blinking patterns between the two eyes. While prior research has used images or videos to identify this disorder, none have specifically targeted the eyes; most require the entire face. A key benefit of our eye-centric approach is that it preserves subject anonymity. Furthermore, our AI relies on straightforward blinking patterns, making the system's decisions explainable and simple. We developed a new feature termed "blink similarity," which quantifies the resemblance between the two eyes' blinking behaviors. Extensive experiments show that this feature is highly robust, enabling effective detection even with limited labeled data. Consequently, our proposed system is both more cost-effective and more convenient than existing methods. In terms of accuracy, our method markedly surpasses current standards. This report examines the causes, symptoms, and diagnostic methods for Bell's Palsy. Following a review of prior research on detection techniques, we present a novel, low-cost, and accurate approach that analyzes eye videos to determine if a subject has Bell's Palsy. Our proposed system leverages the fact that individuals with Bell's Palsy often exhibit different blinking patterns in their left and right eyes. By focusing solely on the eyes, the system is both cost-effective and capable of producing explainable results. Our methodology involves extracting features from each eye and comparing the features of both eyes to assess blinking similarity, thereby detecting the condition. We tested two feature types: 1) traditional features like skewness and entropy, and 2) deep learning-based features utilizing a pre-trained ResNet18 model. We gathered a dataset of eye videos where some subjects had Bell's Palsy and others did not. Our findings indicate that features derived from the ResNet18 model yield the highest accuracy.

The quantum Monte Carlo sign problem hinders the simulation of real-time evolution in interacting many-body systems. Quantum circuits using qudits of size $d$ can be mapped to spin-$\frac{d-1}{2}$ systems with local $SU(d)$ symmetry to bypass this issue. This letter demonstrates that this qudit approach enables efficient real-time simulation of the relativistic $\lambda \phi^4$ theory. We employ random circuit learning to learn $SU(d)$ dynamics generated by a quadratic Hamiltonian and apply this learning to an interacting scalar field theory. We show that these learned dynamics allow for the computation of expectation values and moments in many-body systems, demonstrating that qudit systems are more robust against noise than qubit alternatives.

This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 30% and a charge greater than 30 nC, with a flux of $10^{12}\,{\rm sr}^{-1}$. The degree of polarization varies with deflection angles, reaching up to 60% at specific energies and angles. This angular dependence stems from the asymmetrical laser fields experienced by positrons within the skin layer of the overdense plasma, where radiative spin-flip and radiation reaction are critical factors. Furthermore, this positron polarization is robust and is expected to occur in future 100-PW-class laser-solid experiments, offering diverse application possibilities.

In standard numerical particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations, the self-consistent electromagnetic fields generated by an ultraintense laser pulse interacting with an electron plasma are typically approximated using a macroscopic grid. These simulations rely on a set of macro-particles, where each particle represents $N_b$ real particles, with the plasma described by the collective behavior of these particles rather than individual entities. This study derives an analytical formula for the force exerted on a single micro-particle due to its neighbors, considering both parallel and perpendicular arrangements relative to the plasma density gradient. This formula accounts for plasma screening and validates that the average force on a macro-particle aligns with the self-consistent plasma fields. Furthermore, we introduce a simple algorithm to rapidly update particle positions using this analytical expression instead of the conventional PIC method. Validation shows that this analytical approach yields results identical to those of the standard PIC scheme. Consequently, the approach presented here can be readily applied to replace the standard PIC algorithm in large-scale plasma simulations, potentially improving computational efficiency.

set $S \subseteq G$, the diameter $diam(G,S)$ denotes the smallest integer $n$ such that every element of $G$ can be expressed as a product of at most $n$ elements from $S$. In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. The sensor's front-end utilizes a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to transform local temperature into two biasing currents, which subsequently determine two oscillation frequencies. The ratio of these frequencies corresponds directly to the absolute temperature. The back-end then converts this frequency ratio into a digital temperature code. Benefiting from its low-complexity architecture, the design offers a compact footprint, low power usage, and high accuracy across a broad temperature spectrum. Additionally, an embedded line regulation mechanism enables voltage scalability. Prototyped in 180nm CMOS, the sensor operates within a 0°C to 100°C detection range, supports a supply voltage from 0.6V to 1.8V, and occupies a minimal silicon area of 0.023mm². Experimental results from 20 test chips demonstrate competitive performance metrics, including a resolution of 0.24°C, an inaccuracy of ±1.4°C, a sampling rate of approximately 1.5kHz, and an energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion at 30°C. Furthermore, the sensor delivers a 10-bit temperature code at an energy cost of 2.66pJ per conversion at the same temperature. Finally, a multi-reader scenario involving nine sensors and four readers highlights a potential read-out power optimization of 93.75% when utilizing the proposed scalable design compared to a non-scalable configuration. This sensor reads provide granular thermal data crucial for determining cooling strategies in processors that employ DVFS; a simulation of a 4-way many-core system with 16 readers illustrates a 33.3% improvement in cooling accuracy and a 50% enhancement in system performance (concurrency without thermal throttling) when utilizing this sensor, regardless of whether predictive thermal awareness is employed. Simulated read-out powers for various system and supply voltage configurations at 50°C demonstrate an average of 6.25µW per sensor, equating to just 0.26% of the total power of a 2.4MW sensor array. These power figures represent both the per-sensor consumption and the overall read-out power in multi-sensor systems. The final section of the paper addresses several challenges encountered during the development of this scalable sensor.

While it has been analytically shown that purely toroidal or purely poloidal fields inevitably develop instabilities, numerical simulations confirm that roughly axisymmetric configurations within stably stratified stars can remain stable. These stable setups involve twisted torus structures where toroidal and poloidal components mutually reinforce one another. Previous investigations have estimated approximate upper and lower limits for the ratio of magnetic energy between these two components. To explore the parameter space governing the stability of such configurations, we employed the Pencil Code to conduct 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations of magnetic field evolution in non-rotating, non-degenerate stars, where viscosity serves as the sole dissipation mechanism. Our simulations covered stars with both uniform (barotropic) and radially increasing (stably stratified) specific entropy, varying conditions for the degree of stratification and the magnetic energy distribution. These results broadly corroborate the previously proposed stability boundaries for the magnetic field. Additionally, we constructed a network of ordinary differential equations based on flux conservation to analytically verify the numerical findings regarding magnetic field stability under weak viscosity conditions. For radially stratified stars, the maximum ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic energy was found to scale with the square of the stratification parameter. Configurations with a magnetic energy ratio exceeding $10^4$ ultimately developed an almost purely toroidal component concentrated in the stellar core. Configurations with a ratio below $10^2$ were dominated by a poloidal field, ultimately evolving into a dipole configuration with a unidirectional field at the poles. Configurations with an intermediate ratio displayed the characteristic features of a twisted torus. Furthermore, for initially purely toroidal fields in radially stratified stars, magnetic energy tended to accumulate in the center; however, unlike in degenerate stars, this did not lead to an instability. We also examined the analytical approach by Donati & Landstreet (2006) for separating magnetic components from line-profile analyses of chemically homogeneous, non-degenerate, but rotating and magnetized stars, extending its application to non-rotating stars and verifying its validity against our simulations. Finally, our study supports the hypothesis that the split of crystallisation fronts into two parts on the equatorial plane, as suggested by simulations of degenerate stars, originates from an energy buildup in the core during the stratification phase. This analysis relied on estimating the turnover time of magnetic energy

serves as a versatile method for investigating diverse systems, spanning statistical physics, strong interaction theory, and gravity. Its utility depends on deriving flow equations that track the evolution of the quantum effective action as a coarse-graining parameter varies. This study details a new strategy for solving these equations by leveraging the fact that renormalization group (RG) equations can be reformulated to mirror fluid dynamics conservation laws. This analogy enables two main advancements: first, it permits the use of robust numerical methods from fluid dynamics to solve RG equations, ensuring reliable handling of nonanalytic behaviors in the effective action's flow, such as those arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the fluid dynamics parallel offers fresh perspectives on interpreting RG flows and their inherent irreversibility. We demonstrate this connection using zero-dimensional quantum field theory models, with a discussion of extending it to higher dimensions. These results are anticipated to enhance future FRG investigations of quantum field theories in higher dimensions, improving both qualitative understanding and quantitative accuracy. We further note that this link to fluid dynamics was recently observed in zero-dimensional quantum field theory models within other contexts. This significant parallel between fluid dynamics and renormalization group flows across various quantum field theories holds broader implications for quantum field theory, potentially facilitating connections to other frameworks like lattice field theory, perturbation theory, and conformal field theory.
Zero-dimensional quantum field theories, often termed quantum mechanical models, serve as a crucial testing ground for developing and scrutinizing computational methods capable of accessing the nonperturbative spectrum of Hamiltonians that lack analytical solutions. A primary objective is to validate that the derived RG flows align with the exact spectrum of the corresponding Schrödinger equation. We establish this consistency by examining a supercoset conformal field theory that flows into zero-dimensional quantum field theories. This connection allows us to bridge quantum mechanical RG flows with conformal field theories, revealing a connection between affine Kac-Moody algebras and large-N quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we utilize the relationship between the universal RG beta function and the conformal anomaly to derive the central charge of the corresponding conformal field theory directly from the quantum mechanical Lagrangian.
We investigate renormalization group (RG) flows in supersymmetric (SUSY) quantum mechanics (QM) within a supercoset formulation. Specifically, we analyze the flow of the central charge $c$ and demonstrate that its change across an infrared (IR) fixed point equals the difference in the central charges $c_{UV}$ and $c_{IR}$ of the associated conformal supercosets.

It allows users to query lyrics, song metadata, audio files, or any combination thereof, efficiently delivering relevant results. Furthermore, Pied Piper can generate a consolidated output that links to listenable audio and displays corresponding lyrics and metadata. Potential advantages include reduced exposure to malicious advertisements, enhanced privacy compared to specialized engines, and lower search costs. By leveraging public APIs and open-source tools, Pied Piper operates at a minimal monthly expense of under \$5. API providers such as Spotify, Amazon, and Google often offer free tiers with monthly query limits of approximately 1000; however, this threshold is sufficient for an individual listening 50 songs daily for two weeks or for ten users each listening to 50 songs weekly. The system's source code is openly available on GitHub.

# 1 Introduction
Pied Piper is a meta search engine tailored for music. It produces comprehensive recommendations that facilitate rapid discovery of songs, lyrics, and metadata.

# 2 System Overview
The architecture of Pied Piper is illustrated in Figure 1. It relies on three API providers—Spotify, Amazon, and Google—alongside several open-source projects.

# 3 API Providers and Costs
Pied Piper integrates multiple API services, many of which offer free tiers. For instance, individual accounts on Google Cloud, AWS, and Spotify typically provide about 1000 free queries per month. While 1000 queries might seem restrictive for a search engine, this volume is adequate for a single heavy user listening to 50 songs daily for fourteen days or for ten users (such as a small household) each listening to 50 songs per week. Beyond these free allowances, external search costs are negligible.

# 4 System Design
The core components of the system are detailed in the following sections.

# 4.1 Search Execution
Pied Piper offloads all search operations to three cloud-based API providers.

# 4.2 Data Structures
These sub-sections describe the search algorithms, index, and cache employed to refine API results.

# 4.2.1 Index Algorithm
To supplement API responses, we employ a local index built from publicly accessible text (e.g., blog posts, GitHub repositories, news articles) and audio (primarily YouTube). This index enables the delivery of rich, multi-format search results.

A primary objective in this work is to extend Morita invariance beyond the 1-Lie groupoid level, thereby establishing equivalent structures on stacks. A significant hurdle in this extension is the failure of the standard pullback construction used for defining these equivalences to preserve the structure of 2-Lie groupoids. This limitation arises because the binary 2-morphisms within the pullback 2-Lie groupoid do not fully encompass those of the original 2-Lie groupoids; they are restricted to specific slices defined by the source and target maps of the 1-Lie groupmorhisms. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce a refined definition of the equivalence between 2-Lie groupoids, explicitly incorporating all 2-morphisms of the original 2-Lie groupoids. This new formulation is profoundly linked to the pseudo functors that characterize 2-Lie groupoids, as explored in [arXiv:1907.02513]. In many engineering and scientific fields, analyzing large volumes of 3D point cloud data is both challenging and computationally expensive. While recent advancements in learning algorithms have shown promising results in classifying colored 3D point clouds without explicit feature engineering, these methods rely heavily on the network's capacity, often requiring extensive hyperparameter tuning and computational resources. This work introduces a cost-effective approach that enhances classification accuracy by leveraging context-based feature engineering coupled with dimension reduction techniques. Initially, we engineer features that capture the local geometric context of individual points. subsequently, a selection of machine learning classifiers are trained using these engineered features after they have been processed by various dimension reduction methods. Experimental evaluations across three distinct datasets confirm that our proposed framework outperforms recent state-of-the-art deep learning methods that utilize raw input data, achieving comparable accuracy with significantly lower computational cost. A promising strategy to address this mystery involves correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, as neutrinos directly trace hadronic interactions and remain unaffected by magnetic deflection. This paper outlines three distinct methods for correlating the arrival directions of these particles. Data on neutrinos come from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES, while UHECR data (with energies exceeding ~50 EeV) are sourced from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. Both datasets offer enhanced statistics and refined reconstructions compared to our 2015 findings. The first analysis employs a high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source detection to identify excesses of neutrinos clustering near UHECR trajectories. The second method looks for an excess of UHECRs pointing toward the highest-energy neutrinos, while the third examines excesses of UHECR-neutrino pairs across various angular scales. No significant excesses were detected in any of these analyses, and previously reported over-fluctuations have seen their statistical significance diminished. Consequently, these results allow for tighter constraints on the spatially correlated neutrino flux associated with UHECRs. Ultimately, these findings underscore the necessity of data from future experiments with greater sensitivity.

By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Our stress data aligns with established models for the slippage and anchored regimes, while we introduce a leverage rule to characterize stresses during stick-slip events. Furthermore, we determine that the transition between stick-slip and anchored regimes is governed by a roughness factor, defined as the ratio of surface asperity size to the radius of curvature of the Plateau borders. This factor functions as a novel dimensionless roughness metric for solid-liquid interfaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that the slippage regime extends to higher Reynolds numbers when surface asperities are macroscopic. From an interface hydrodynamics perspective, our findings indicate that interfacial roughness can spontaneously induce multiple flow regimes. These insights are broadly applicable to complex fluid systems involving interfaces, offering new experimental methods to quantify roughness and spontaneous flow behaviors at solid-liquid boundaries.

At the outset of COVID-19 lockdowns during the first half of 2020, we initiated a study into the link between voluntary individual behaviors and the subsequent evolution of the epidemic curve. Utilizing data from two large-scale online surveys conducted in Italy—we examined the impact of specific constraints on the epidemic's shape in their absence. First, we quantified the reduction in mass mobility resulting from the closure of non-essential shops and services, showing that this closure alone could have caused a factor-of-10 slowdown in the epidemic's growth phase. Second, we analyzed the voluntary adherence to social distancing measures among isolated individuals. We demonstrated that a decrease in compliant individuals by just 10% could have produced a 2-fold amplification of the epidemic curve's peak. These results underscore the potential for carefully designed, scalable, and cost-effective questionnaires to provide real-time estimates of the impact of voluntary behavioral changes on the epidemic trajectory, thereby offering valuable inputs for optimizing the timing of policy interventions.

We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving mixed modes and circumferentially localized folds, varying with rotation rate and external pressure. The analysis includes both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral configurations, with results illustrated through bifurcation diagrams. Furthermore, the ratio of the system scale to the natural length scale is identified as the key factor governing the sequence of primary bifurcations from the unperturbed circular state, as well as the resulting solution profiles and the initiation of secondary bifurcations. Solutions are visualized to clarify the flow and deformation dynamics driving these phenomena and to compare the inextensible and extensible membrane systems. These extensible membrane state equations align closely with prior experimental observations by Park and Park (J. Fluid Mech. 840, E16, 2018), suggesting that the analyzed primary bifurcation sequences represent a fundamental mechanism in Hele-Shaw finger spreading. Finally, the extensible membrane state equations are expressed in terms of a single dimensionless group, extending the findings into regimes of strong swelling where the dominant length scale approaches the system scale. These results offer insights into the extended primary bifurcation sequences observed experimentally. This approach may also serve as a foundation for investigating spatially localized defects, such as pinholes, and for extending the study to soluble membranes.

In these scenarios, the counts of initial and final microstates differ, preventing connection via unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This issue frequently arises when phase space volume changes and has not previously been examined using Hamiltonian trajectories capable of being inverted to create an identity mapping between microstates as Hamiltonian parameters vary. To address this challenge, we propose a specific technique, focusing on free expansion within an isolated system where the notion of dissipated work remains ambiguous. Our approach demonstrates thermodynamic consistency and offers significant utility for simulations. We provide justification that the dissipated quantity corresponds to the thermodynamic average of internal microwork performed by a microstate; this internal microwork differs from exchange microwork with the vacuum, which is zero. Furthermore, we establish that microwork remains nonnegative during free expansion—a notable finding, given that its sign is not fixed in general processes. Finally, we address criticisms raised against this method in a recent publication. The adiabatic segment allows the equation of state to asymptotically approach two distinct power laws, effectively interpolating between dust and dark energy regimes at early and late cosmic epochs. The dissipative component features a bulk viscosity with a constant coefficient. Utilizing phase space analysis, we robustly characterize the model's dynamical behavior without relying on explicit system solutions. Model parameters are constrained by both asymptotic behaviors and extensive observational data. We numerically solve the Hubble parameter equation, plotting results against the latest Hubble data. Furthermore, the $Om(z)$ test confirms that, despite being quintessence-like, the model traverses the phantom barrier. We examine the universe's evolution by analyzing the deceleration parameter, cosmic density, the effective equation of state, and the underlying dark energy properties. The estimated present-day viscosity coefficient is $8 \times 10^6 Pa.s$, consistent with previous studies by Velten and Schwartz [26], Wang and Meng [27], and Sasidharan and Mathew [29]. We conclude that this model successfully accounts for the observed evolution of the universe.

Although many educational systems inadvertently diminish curiosity by prioritizing test preparation, educators are increasingly focused on methods to stimulate it, recognizing the necessity of lifelong learning and reskilling in the future. Despite this, the influence of peers in triggering curiosity remains underexplored. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework offering an integrated socio-cognitive perspective that links observable peer behaviors to internal curiosity states. While numerous Gaussian process models exist for Euclidean input spaces, options for undirected graph inputs are significantly more restricted. This study utilizes the stochastic partial differential equation formulation of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes—a popular model in Euclidean contexts—to develop their corresponding analogs for undirected graphs. Existing sensing methods, which rely on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data from commuters (such as Google Maps), suffer from significant drawbacks, including high costs, restricted coverage, and low reliability due to insufficient user participation. This study explores an innovative drive-by sensing approach that utilizes large-scale ridesourcing vehicles (RVs) to monitor and infer the status of urban road networks. By analyzing the performance of the RV fleet, we evaluate metrics such as the unique number of road segments visited, sensing reliability derived from repeated visits, and the implicit information inferable from explicit data combined with network topology. We introduce an optimal rerouting model designed to simultaneously maximize both sensing coverage and reliability, which can be efficiently solved using a heuristic algorithm to sequentially guide the trajectories of unoccupied RVs. To validate the model's effectiveness, comprehensive experiments and sensitivity analyses were conducted using real-world data from over 20,000 RVs in New York City. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach visits approximately 43% of all road segments, covering 80% of high-traffic segments (exceeding 1,000 daily trips), with an inferred coverage of nearly 96%. Furthermore, when focusing on coverage and reliability within a 15-minute window, this method visits 61% of road segments, with an inferred coverage of 91%. In terms of cost-effectiveness, the proposed approach visits 3.6 times more road segments than inductive loop sensors installed at intersections and 1.5 times more than those placed in the middle of road segments. To enhance sensing and inference capabilities, strategies for incorporating external data sources and employing machine learning techniques are also discussed. Ultimately, this work highlights the vast potential of leveraging ridesourcing vehicles for urban transportation management. To further facilitate such applications, we have released all datasets and code used in this study as open-source resources.

Utilizing low-energy effective field theories (EFTs) to model general neutrino interactions and Dirac fermion DM coupled to charm quarks, we conduct likelihood fits fitting the experimental non-observation of $J/\psi$ disappearance at the Belle II collider. For neutrinos, we establish novel sensitivity to sub-GeV masses across numerous decay channels and all EFT operators, with $J/\psi\to e^+e^-\gamma$ proving particularly effective for sub-GeV masses between 400 MeV and 1 GeV. Regarding Dirac DM, we explore complementary constraints from $J/\psi$ decays, covering mass regimes from $\mathcal{O}(1)$ MeV to 1 GeV. We further compare these limits with those from other experiments, highlighting the significance of precision $J/\psi$ measurements for probing sub-GeV DM. Finally, we examine how future DM production searches at the Belle II factory influence these constraints. Given the anticipated sensitivity of upcoming experiments such as TOMODI and NA65 at SPS-based DM detectors, we demonstrate that current sub-GeV Dirac DM EFT operators remain unprobed. Additionally, we show how to incorporate DM scattering off electrons and nucleons into the global fit; even for small cross-sections, the high flux of $J/\psi$ produced at Belle II renders this framework highly sensitive. We conclude by extending this analysis to other $J/\psi$ experiments. The findings of this work inform future comprehensive global fits of sub-GeV DM effective field theories. systems are widely deployed by governments and testing agencies to assess millions of candidates on high-stakes matters, including university admissions and visa eligibility. Despite this prevalence, there is a scarcity of research dedicated to interpreting the opaque nature of these deep-learning algorithms. Existing studies suggest that such scoring models are easily manipulable. This paper investigates the causes of their surprising adversarial brittleness. Leveraging recent interpretability advancements, we examine the relative importance of features like coherence, content, vocabulary, and relevance in automated scoring. We analyze the phenomena of oversensitivity (where minor input changes cause significant score fluctuations) and overstability (where major input changes yield minimal score shifts). Our findings reveal that, despite being trained as "end-to-end" models with rich contextual embeddings like BERT, AES models function similarly to bag-of-words models. A few isolated words often dictate the final score without necessitating context, rendering the models largely overstable. This contrasts sharply with recent probing studies on pre-trained language models, which demonstrate their ability to encode complex linguistic features such as morphology and parts of speech. Furthermore, we observe that these models have internalized dataset biases, leading to oversensitivity. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose detection-based protection models capable of identifying samples exhibiting oversensitivity and overstability while maintaining high accuracy. Our experiments across three datasets and three scoring models demonstrate that these models achieve an F-score of 90% in detecting overstability and an oversensitivity detection F-score of 87%. These insights feature engineering and scoring models to create more reliable and transparent AES systems. The source code for the protection models is available at https://github.com/PranavAnand27/Brittle-AES-Models.

(IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 0.1 meters in length and 0.4 meters in diameter, generates the required plasma environment ahead of the ICRF antenna. This source, which features a helical antenna, was engineered to achieve a helicon discharge mode. Although it was previously unconfirmed whether the source could reach this mode, achieving helicon operation is crucial for maximizing the source's capacity and producing high-density plasma. Consequently, a comprehensive study was conducted to attain helicon mode. This involved characterizing key plasma parameters—such as electron temperature, density, and plasma potential—and implementing a global model for particle and power balance. The study confirmed the existence of helicon mode at magnetic fields below 35 mT. To achieve the maximum possible plasma density, an optimization strategy was proposed to enable helicon mode operation at the highest available magnetic field. Final remarks address potential pathways for enhancing both the achieved and theoretical maximum plasma density. Initially, the source suffered from significant maintenance issues; these are detailed along with their potential resolutions and the potential for improving the source's future performance. Additionally, several aspects regarding the source's installation are discussed, including challenges and solutions related to extracting high-power S-band signals from the magnetized environment. Finally, measurements from a survey inside the S-band antenna cavity are presented. Measuring these parameters is essential for accurately calibrating the probes used to determine the electric field vector within the antenna.

In contemporary times, various strategies and approaches are being explored to manage and suppress pest outbreaks. Entomopathogenic nematodes, which act as biological control agents, infect target insects and deliver microbial pathogens that not only eliminate existing adults but also inhibit the birth rate of immature stages (larvae and nymphs). This dual action of mortality and sublethal inhibition helps slow the development of resistance and enhances the potential for effective pest control.

Nucleus segmentation technology is commonly employed to automate these tasks; however, training robust segmentation models remains challenging due to issues like nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive background fusion. Although recent approaches based on point annotation have significantly enhanced model performance, they still require experienced pathologists to provide the necessary annotations. Unlike traditional U-Net-based methods that directly map pathology images to target masks, our approach decomposes the detection task into two sub-tasks: first mapping the original image to a binary mask, and then mapping that binary mask to a density mask. This task splitting significantly reduces complexity and enhances the network's overall performance. Extensive experiments on the PDC2019 dataset demonstrate the model's superiority, with our automatic detection model achieving an IoU of 0.7355 and a MAE of 20.5358 in path length calculation. These results validate the model's potential for cancer diagnosis assistance and highlight its advantages over existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengjintu/PDC2019-Wshaped-detection-Model. Our approach offers several key contributions to pathological image analysis. First, the proposed W-shaped network innovatively reduces task complexity by splitting detection into two sub-tasks, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods. Second, this work introduces an automatic nucleus detection algorithm designed to reduce manual labor, lower reliance on high-quality annotated data, and assist pathologists in making more efficient and accurate diagnoses. Third, our model supports cancer diagnosis through nucleus measurement and path length calculation, with experimental results confirming its competitiveness against state-of-the-art solutions. Finally, the proposed W-shaped network demonstrates strong generalization across different staining types and image sizes. These findings provide valuable insights and practical value for pathological image analysis. Our code and models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhengjintu/PDC2019-Wshaped-detection-Model.

Infection with SARS-CoV-2 can initiate pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory cell death mechanism, via the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway. The formation of this inflammasome may lead to cell death, a outcome that anti-inflammatory drugs are capable of preventing. This study presents an intracellular model of NLRP3 inflammasome development, pyroptosis, and various anti-inflammatory interventions. The findings demonstrate that these medications can shift cell death from pyroptosis to apoptosis. Furthermore, in conjunction with the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator created by a multidisciplinary team, this model enables the investigation of combined therapeutic effects at the tissue level. This document highlights pyroptosis and its connection to the cellular death dynamics simulated by the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator. Therefore, the insights gained from multi-scale models of this infection can inform strategies for anti-inflammatory treatments. Additionally, the intracellular model described here is accessible on the simulator's website.

This paper presents HELMHOLTZ, a type-based static verification tool designed for Michelson, the statically typed, stack-based language used to write smart contracts on the Tezos blockchain. Built upon an extension of Michelson's type system featuring refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accepts Michelson programs annotated with user-defined specifications expressed as refinement types. Additionally, the authors provide a formal specification of their refined type system for Michelson and present a prototype implementation of this system.

This work revisits GCNN operations to demonstrate that their convolution layers function as matched filters, aligning input data with specific patterns or features. By adopting this matched filter perspective, we offer a unified explanation of GCNNs, extending the framework to include nonlinear ReLU and max-pooling layers. In many machine learning applications, particularly when dealing with sensor networks or spatiotemporal data like video or social images, data points exist in high- or infinite-dimensional spaces that are correlated through spatial or temporal relationships. GCNNs were specifically designed to process such data. While the term "graph convolution" is widely recognized in deep learning communities, a rigorous mathematical definition has historically been missing. Recent graph signal processing techniques have defined convolution as a localized operation in the spatial domain, analogous to how multiplication functions locally on a graph. Building on this foundation, this study provides a comprehensive explanation of GCNN operations—covering message passing, learned parameters, and the learning process themselves—through the lens of localized operations and matched filters. This approach not only clarifies the black-box nature of GCNNs but also connects them to traditional convolutional neural networks and fully connected networks.

Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) represent a recent advancement in processing data structured as graphs or manifolds. While GCNs exhibit performance comparable to fully connected neural networks, their parameter efficiency is significantly higher. Despite their utility in classification and regression tasks, many practitioners lack a thorough understanding of how GCNs process data. This work investigates the operational mechanics of GCNs, offering an intuitive interpretation of their graph convolution based on the theory of matched filters and localization. This perspective enables a clearer understanding of how information propagates across the network

In this work, we construct solutions to the equations of motion for a complex scalar field with a specific self-interaction term within Abelian Jackiw-Templeton (JT) gravity. This framework involves two non-Abelian gauge groups with opposite sign quadratic Casimir operators, where one group possesses a mass term while the other does not. When the massive group's Casimir is coupled to the scalar field and the mass-degenerate group is coupled to gravity, the resulting field equations yield solutions with negative entropy. By switching to the dual description of the JT gravity sector, we derive solutions with positive energy and entropy. Specifically, we examine the stability of these boson stars under radial perturbations. While our model allows for the generation of positive energy and entropy, the associated solutions prove to be unstable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the differential equation governing linear perturbations exhibits a non-terminating infinite series of zeros.

The relationship between these two concepts can be defined by the equation: imperative algorithms equal proofs with cuts. This insight motivates a broader generalization of pseudocode, termed *logical pseudocodes*, which parallels natural deduction proofs within computability logic \cite{Jap03,Jap08}. In this system, every statement maps directly to a specific step in a natural deduction proof. Consequently, the primary advantage of logical pseudocodes over traditional pseudocode is the assurance that each statement adheres to correctness and safety relative to the initial specifications. Furthermore, this approach represents an extension of the computability logic web (\colw) that incorporates forward reasoning capabilities. The accompanying software tool, LogicP (\colp), facilitates the creation of natural deduction proofs from forward-reasoning pseudocode and renders them interactive. Additionally, LogicP supports the verification of assertions made about forward-looking statements; these assertions can range from simple preconditions and postconditions to complex invariants and loop guards. By employing invariants, users can build upon prior work more effectively, thereby enabling modular correctness arguments. It is important to note that LogicP is complementary to, rather than a replacement for, the Computation Logic Web (\colw). The following resources demonstrate this integration:
-   The Correctness Logic Web (\clw) allows users to read correctness proofs written in logical pseudocode from \colw, alongside their associated algorithms.
-   The Computation Logic Web with Cuts (\colwc) enables readers of standard pseudocode (cuts) to traverse to corresponding correctness proofs found in the Correctness Logic Web.

-   The software tool LogicP (\colp) supports both forward reasoning and modular correctness arguments by facilitating the writing of natural deduction proofs.
-   LogicP (\colp) can be downloaded from Colap (\colp).

# A Memory-Efficient CycleGAN for Low-Dose CT Denoising

Low-dose computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation exposure by decreasing X-ray tube current or the number of detector rows, which consequently increases image noise and degrades quality. Deep learning has recently emerged as a effective super-resolution technique for converting low-dose images to routine-dose ones. While cycleGAN offers an advantageous unsupervised solution by eliminating the need for matched high-dose references, it is limited by its need for two generators during training to ensure cycle-consistency, despite requiring just one during inference. This paper presents **AdaCycleGAN**, which utilizes a single switchable generator equipped with AdaIN layers to enforce cycle-consistency through simple dose-level switching. Unlike cycleGAN, our proposed **AdaCycleGAN** reduces parameter count by approximately half while delivering superior memory efficiency and performance. Our results indicate that the new architecture outperforms existing cycleGAN methods while using roughly half the parameters, even when trained on limited datasets. This efficient design can be easily integrated into other deep learning frameworks for low-dose CT reconstruction, potentially improving their memory usage and performance.

Pre-trained language models have recently advanced dialog understanding, yet current methods rely on supervised contrastive objectives tied to specific prediction tasks and lack help with external metrics like coreference resolution. We propose utilizing auxiliary discrimination losses derived from external evaluations to supplement standard supervised pre-training. Specifically, we develop a framework that incorporates objectives from tasks assessing coreference resolution and coherent summarization to improve coreference handling and overall context coherence. This approach, named CoDiLLa (Context-Coherent Dialogue Pre-training with Dual-objective Contrastive Learning), was tested on English and multilingual datasets. Results show CoDiLLa significantly outperforms recent state-of-the-art methods in coreference resolution and coherent summarization.

Recent advancements in dialog understanding rely on predicting immediate utterances, but these tasks fail to capture long-range discourse structures or align with coreference resolution needs. This work examines coreference resolution and summarization tasks to construct a CoDiLLa framework that enhances dialogue coherence. By performing joint contrastive learning on coreference and summarization objectives, the model learns to place similar speakers' utterances closer together and preserves more information when compressing dialogue sequences. This approach leverages external evaluations to prevent overfitting to superficial task characteristics.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents achieve better results by training on a set of similar tasks, utilizing their shared features to address a wider range of problems. While such implicit relatedness is easily assumed in model-free methods due to a single policy network covering all tasks, it creates ambiguity in model-based approaches. We investigate how the shared dynamics model influences implicit task relatedness and propose a structured modeling approach that enhances performance in multi-task settings.

Model-based multi-task reinforcement learning enhances an agent's sample efficiency by embedding explicit task structure, allowing it to learn multiple tasks simultaneously from limited experience. However, we identify that this method can suffer from implicit task confusion when a single dynamics network is used across all tasks. To address this, we introduce a structured modeling architecture that improves implicit task relatedness without adding extra parameters. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields significant performance gains in both gridworld and 3D control environments.

We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. Assuming the screens remained relatively stable over this period, we modeled variations in arc curvature across Earth's orbit to determine the position, orientation, and velocity of five of the six screens. Our most precise distance measurement places one screen at $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from Earth, which we associate with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble. Furthermore, combining data from multiple pulsars with similar geometries allows us to track the evolution of these screens along their trajectories. We demonstrate that the closest screen is consistent with the progression of a density wave from a supernova $\sim$2 kpc away, implying an ambient shock velocity of $\sim$100 km/s within a hot ($T \sim 8000$ K) intercloud medium. Additionally, we provide an overview of all available screens for pulsars situated beyond the local volume and propose that many of these screens, or a significant portion of them, can be attributed to the progression of density waves from nearby supernovae. This study contributes to developing a general model for pulsar scintillation screens, characterized by the progression of solar wind magnetic field structures.

(QPNet), a pitch-adaptive generative model designed to enhance the limited pitch controllability of standard WaveNet (WN) through the use of pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). While WN, a probabilistic autoregressive model utilizing stacked dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio synthesis, its reliance solely on data without prior audio knowledge hampers its ability to control pitch. Specifically, WN struggles to accurately generate periodic audio components when provided with auxiliary fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features that fall outside the range present in the training data. To overcome these limitations, QPNet employs two innovative approaches: first, it integrates PDCNNs to dynamically adjust the WN architecture based on the input auxiliary $F_{0}$, and second, it adopts a cascaded network structure to jointly model the long- and short-term dependencies inherent in quasi-periodic signals like speech. Evaluations on single-tone sinusoids and speech demonstrate that the proposed method effectively handles unseen auxiliary $F_{0}$ values and improves speech generation through the cascaded design. Experiments with 16-kHz sampled speech further show that QPNet produces more natural sounding speech with superior perceptual $F_{0}$ control compared to WN, even when the auxiliary $F_{0}$ values are entirely new and were not included in the training data. For a corpus of 100k utterances, the two-step fine-tuning process required approximately 30 minutes on a single GPU. Due to its capacity to handle auxiliary $F_{0}$ values of any fundamental frequency and its compatibility with various other audio tasks, this work serves as a foundational step toward more intelligent audio generative models. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhihantau/QuasiPeriodicWaveNet.

Our primary technical advancement demonstrates that training a network to explicitly distinguish challenging image fragments—even when the sound-emitting object is present—substantially enhances localization accuracy. We achieve this by introducing an elegant mechanism that automatically mines hard samples and integrates them into a contrastive learning framework. Deep learning has seen rapid advancements in video-based action recognition, yet constructing large-scale datasets with fine-grained action annotations remains difficult. Existing approaches typically rely on temporal attention modules that generate scalar scores for video segments, making it difficult to determine precise action boundaries. We introduce ActionSet, the first 10 million-scale video dataset specifically designed for action boundary classification and subsequent regression. Our construction process involves two key steps: 1) generating action-set candidates by classifying short clips at various boundaries using off-the-shelf action recognition models, and 2) expanding the dataset by mining diverse positive and negative candidates from YouTube and other large-scale video repositories based on the characteristics of the initial 50 million candidates from Twitter. We develop a boundary classification model based on Inception-Temporal Network (ITN) that explicitly minimizes the Softmax cross-entropy loss among positive and negative candidates for each video to train the system. Experimental results indicate that our model significantly outperforms strong baselines in both binary classification and regression tasks. We release the dataset and code at https://github.com/yzhl1999/ActionSet.

significant recent interest. While most GCNs operate within Euclidean geometry, this approach often leads to high distortion when embedding graphs with scale-free or hierarchical structures. To address this, recent models have been developed to function in non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic geometry. Although hyperbolic GCNs demonstrate promising results, current hyperbolic graph operations fail to strictly adhere to hyperbolic geometry, potentially limiting the space's utility and degrading model performance. This paper introduces a novel hyperbolic GCN, the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which ensures that learned node features rigorously conform to hyperbolic geometry. Specifically, we reconstruct key hyperbolic graph operations, such as feature transformation and non-linear activation, using their Lorentzian counterparts. Additionally, we propose an efficient neighborhood aggregation method grounded in Lorentzian distance centroids. We further demonstrate the equivalence of these proposed operations across different types of hyperbolic geometry, providing fundamental proof of their correctness. Experiments across six datasets reveal that LGCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods and exhibits lower distortion when learning representations for tree-like graphs compared to existing hyperbolic GCNs. Furthermore, we observe that replacing standard graph operations with those defined in this paper can enhance the performance of certain existing hyperbolic GCNs. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zirui-Zhang/LGCN.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have produced various models capable of processing graph-structured data, yet their effectiveness relies heavily on data dimensions. Existing efforts have explored manifolds like hyperbolic space to handle tree-like data, but no general graph method exists for other dimensions. This work presents a solution utilizing graph signal processing (SP) techniques applicable across all dimensions. We introduce the General Dimension-adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (GDGCN), which leverages SP operations to extract features from both dimensions and embedded graph structures. Our general framework aggregates nodes through a stack of dimension-gcns, enabling the extraction of joint features from data whether it is scalar, embedded within a manifold, or represented as a graph. Consequently, our method outperforms specialized models designed for specific data types across diverse tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and translation prediction.

# Introduction

The interaction of light with matter is fundamental to many areas of science and technology, driving significant progress in sensing, imaging, and more [1–3]. As quantum technologies advance, interacting quantum systems are anticipated to revolutionize science by expanding the frontiers of precision measurement [4–6], searching for new physics [7–9], enhancing optical sensing [10–12], improving mass sensing [13–15], and facilitating quantum noise reduction [16–18]. Noise arises from the inherent stochastic nature of quantum measurement interactions; for instance, quantum optics experiments exhibit shot noise [19], while macroscopic mechanical systems are subject to thermal noise [16]. Reducing or transferring specific noise types from one system to another is crucial for constructing ultra-sensitive quantum sensors and performing quantum limited measurements.

By integrating this hybrid system, we can transfer noise from the mechanical member to the optical cavity, thereby achieving thermal noise reduction on the mechanical component [16–18].

Although first-order logic with least and greatest fixed points offers powerful succinctness for specifying program properties, its current practical implementations are often limited by the undecidability of model checking on structures with atoms or by high complexity on finite domains. Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. The study of gravitational waves within the Solar System has historically relied on the LIGO detection framework, which was constructed using the standard weak field approximation of General Relativity. This approach relies on the propagation of transverse, traceless gravitational waves at the speed of light. However, an alternative framework can be developed within a local, flat-spacetime formulation of linearized massive gravity. This massive framework is defined by the Lagrangian for the harmonic gauge. Within this context, the transverse condition imposed on the metric perturbation allows the speed of gravitational waves to vary from the speed of light in a controlled manner. This framework offers a potential explanation for the recently observed gravitational wave event GW170815 and its associated electromagnetic signal GN2015. While the amplitude of this event can be attributed to neutron star mergers, its unusual properties are linked to the non-transverse nature of the gravitational wave generated in this model. Notably, the group velocity of these waves exceeds the speed of light. Additionally, the model predicts that the wavefronts of local gravitational waves will assume a sharp edge.

The theory of homomorphisms for signed graphs is a recent advancement that deepens the link between graph coloring and minor theories. Building on this, we explore the relationship via the concept of Extended Double Covers of signed graphs, introduced recently by Naserasr, Sopena, and Zaslavsky. Specifically, a signed graph $(B, \pi)$ is termed \emph{planar-complete} if every planar signed graph $(G, \sigma)$ satisfying the conditions of a fundamental no-homomorphism lemma relative to $(B,\pi)$ possesses a homomorphism to $(B, \pi)$. We propose the conjecture that if a connected signed graph $(B, \pi)$ containing no positive odd closed walk is planar-complete, then its Extended Double Cover ${\rm EDC}(B,\pi)$ is likewise planar-complete. This conjecture significantly generalizes the Four-Color Theorem and is closely tied to several conjectures extending this landmark result. A signed graph $(B,\pi)$ \emph{bounds} a class of graphs if every member of that class admits a homomorphism to $(B,\pi)$. Supporting our conjecture, we establish it for the subclass of signed $K_4$-minor free graphs. Motivated by the initial proof, which relied on orienting edges in an appropriate way, we formulate a stronger version of the conjecture that explicitly includes the claim of edge orientation. Finally, we define a class of signed planar graphs named \emph{almost-bipartite} that is strictly larger than the class of signed bipartite graphs. Although it remains unknown whether all signed bipartite graphs are planar-complete within the context of signed planar graphs, we demonstrate that this unknown question remains unresolved even when restricting the class of signed bipartite graphs to those that bound almost-bipartite graphs. This counterintuitive finding suggests that the property of having a homomorphism to a particular signed bipartite graph does not necessarily imply adjacent vertices can be merged while preserving a homomorphism to an extended double cover of that signed bipartite graph. Throughout our work, we present numerous examples and counterexamples, some of which illustrate that certain conditions in our conjecture and its stronger variant cannot be relaxed. This characterization depends on analyzing tissue samples histologically to assess malignancy and the degree of dysplasia. Although deep neural networks demonstrate remarkable accuracy in recognizing medical patterns, they necessitate extensive sets of annotated training images. We present UniToPatho, a curated dataset comprising 9,536 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed to facilitate the training of deep neural networks for colorectal polyp classification and adenoma grading. We propose a novel framework consisting of three components to perform semantic segmentation on lung CT images: (1) a three-stage data augmentation technique combining rotation, scaling, and intensity adjustments; (2) the initialization of network weights through superpixel-based clustering; and (3) the adoption of the U-Net architecture. We conduct experiments comparing our approach against various data augmentations and initialization strategies across three public datasets. These evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves superior semantic segmentation results with faster convergence and reduced computational cost compared to existing solutions. We further release our code and models open-source at https://github.com/SebastianRivas/Segmentation_Lung.

We introduce a new approach for semantic segmentation of liver and tumor regions in abdominal CT scans, leveraging the DenseVol3D network. This architecture functions as fully convolutional siamese networks, enabling efficient, low-computation inference while delivering state-of-the-art accuracy. Our method also incorporates careful data augmentation and ensembling techniques. Results from two public datasets show that our approach attains high IoU scores with significantly fewer labeled samples than previously required. Our code and models are available at https://lvaldes.github.io/LS2022/.

While applicable across all frequencies $\omega$, the method demonstrates particular efficiency in high-frequency scenarios. Built upon a time-domain framework, the approach comprises three stages: \emph{i)} generating an incoming plane wavelet with compact support along the propagation direction; \emph{ii)} resolving the scattering event in the time domain for this wavelet; and \emph{iii)} recovering the time-harmonic solution through a temporal Fourier transform of the time-domain result. A critical component is a front-tracking mesh adaptation algorithm employed in stage \emph{ii)}. By leveraging the localized nature of the wave front, this strategy significantly reduces the dependency of the required degrees of freedom on the frequency $\omega$ to achieve a specified accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a specialized algorithm for the Fourier transform in stage \emph{iii)} that capitalizes on the reduced degrees of freedom inherent to the adapted meshes. Numerical tests validate the method's advantages and confirm its applicability to external source terms, including point sources and sound-soft scatterers. However, the achieved efficiency is constrained when trapping modes are present. Notably, the proposed approach yields solutions of comparable accuracy to conventional methods while requiring substantially fewer degrees of freedom.

Although widely utilized, the backpropagation technique for estimating source locations from scattered acoustic fields has not previously been rigorous. This paper addresses that gap by rigorously analyzing the convergence of source location estimates as the SNRE regularization parameter approaches zero and as the wavenumber increases. This analysis reveals that, without regularization, the convergence rate for the angle of incidence is only $O(k^{-1/2})$. To address this, we propose a novel regularization scheme that achieves the optimal convergence rate of $O(k^{-1})$. Additionally, we examine the application of this method to locating multiple inhomogeneities and determine that it remains effective provided the scattered acoustic fields do not exhibit constructive interference. Finally, numerical experiments illustrate the benefits of the new scheme in source localization and demonstrate its utility in determining the position, orientation, and strength of time-harmonic point sources.

The deuterium enrichment relative to solar values varies significantly, ranging from factor of 1.6 to 3.6 among Group D samples, while the Group E sample exhibits a lower enrichment of approximately factor of 1.3. Conversely, water contents vary widely, from approximately 0.6 to 2.4 wt.% in Group D samples and about 0.3 wt.% in Group E. Although these properties display substantial heterogeneity, they can be effectively accounted for if the samples originated from a parent body with primordial solar-composition water that underwent thermal metamorphism or metamorphic metamorphism, including self-sustained reactions like thermal catalytic hydrogen loss. In this context, we define these processes as "planetary processing." Such thermal events can partially explain the solar-like isotopic ratio observed in GRS070408 and the enhanced ratios in other samples, which likely resulted from kinetic catalytic hydrogen loss during thermal metamorphism; the magnitude of this enrichment is expected to increase with lower initial water contents. Finally, we determined that roughly 10^18 J of energy would be needed to metamorphose ~10 km^-scale parent bodies from solar-composition ice+rock mixtures to reproduce the observed hydrogen isotopic ratios and water contents in GRS070408 and a model case of Group D samples, respectively. These findings offer new insights into the diversity of cometary physical and chemical properties, as well as their formation and evolution within the solar nebula and subsequent dynamical history. While end-to-end architectures aim to eliminate this by utilizing a single system, they are hindered by a lack of sufficient training data. This study investigates combining large-scale ASR and MT models with relatively small-scale ST models through domain adaptation via minimum risk decoding (MRD). Our findings indicate that this hybrid approach necessitates significantly less training data compared to standard end-to-end methods while delivering comparable performance. Additionally, the proposed method outperforms both the baseline end-to-end model and a cascaded system that uses an ASR model without adaptation, demonstrating that MRD-based combination more effectively mitigates domain shifts and domain mismatches in low-resource settings. However, it is noted that MRD slightly underperforms in multilingual contexts rich in multidomain data. Ultimately, this research offers practical insights for selecting between end-to-end and hybrid ST approaches based on specific task requirements.

**Abstract:** This paper examines integrating large-scale Automatic Speech Recognition and Machine Translation models with smaller models for Speech Translation (ST) tasks via minimum risk decoding (MRD) during domain adaptation. The method achieves significant improvements over unadapted end-to-end systems and cascaded pipelines that rely solely on unadapted ASR. By leveraging transfer learning, the proposed approach requires substantially less training data than typical end-to-end systems while delivering similar results, highlighting the advantages and limitations of such hybrid configurations in low-resource and multilingual domains.

Although state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures have been developed, they require extensive training data, creating a challenge for applications with limited resources. We investigate combining large-scale ASR and MT models with smaller, unadapted ST models using minimum risk decoding (MRD) during domain adaptation

We determine that spherical multipoles are most effective for modeling the scattering of electromagnetic radiation, a finding demonstrated using an amorphous silicon sphere. Subsequently, these multipoles are applied to compute the optical forces exerted on semiconductor, dielectric, and metallic particles across a broad spectrum of wavelengths, spanning from the dipolar to the Mie regimes. Results indicate that irreducible Cartesian multipoles yield accurate optical force predictions within a specific range relative to the particle size, whereas spherical multipoles remain accurate over all size regimes. Finally, we propose a strategy to enhance the optimal sizing range of irreducible multipoles or to extend the application of spherical multipoles to smaller particles. These findings are anticipated to aid researchers in selecting appropriate microparticle models for conducting optical tweezers experiments. This research was supported by grant No. 315986 from the Science and Technology Research Council of Chile (ANID). In Appendix A, we present an analytical derivation of the optical force expressed through spherical multipoles, which has been made available since October 2022 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7723484. The core methodology of this paper was also published openly since October 2022 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7723475.
Although prior research has established that spherical multipoles are highly efficient for predicting optical forces on small particles, no study has previously determined their effective particle size range. This work investigates the maximum particle size for which spherical multipoles can accurately predict optical forces across three distinct regimes. Utilizing a numerical approach based on the null-field expansion method, we demonstrate that spherical multipoles are exceptionally well-suited for modeling optical trapping of semiconductor and dielectric particles in the Mie regime, specifically for particles with a diameter up to approximately ten wavelengths. Furthermore, we show that these multipoles are ineffective for modeling optical absorption and heating in metallic particles in the dipolar regime. Although irreducible multipoles offer accurate predictions for optical forcing, they require significant modifications to be effective in the Mie regime. These conclusions are expected to assist experimentalists in determining the suitability of computational models for predicting optical trapping and manipulation effects on microparticles in optical tweezers experiments. symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Finally, we propose signature channels at the Large Hadron Collider and examine the discoverability of the model, noting that success hinges on the nature of dark matter. We identify an optimal scenario characterized by quasi-degenerate heavy neutrinos, featuring resonant production of long-lived particles that constitute "beams" along specific trajectories. This results in distinct experimental signatures, such as secondary vertices with displaced photons or charged hadrons, potentially offering an alternative explanation for the muon-like anomalies observed at the LHC. The findings are supported by supplementary data provided in two public notebooks on GitHub.

Discovered neutrino oscillations imply that neutrinos possess non-zero masses, yet the Standard Model's mechanism for generating these sub-eV masses remains unclear. We propose that the spectral distortion known as the muon-bump can be explained by long-lived dark matter produced via resonances. Specifically, we demonstrate that extending the Scoto-SeeSaw model to include a simple singlet fermion scenario allows it to accommodate neutrino oscillation data, explain the muon-bump anomaly, and generate a self-consistent dark matter candidate.

Although three neutrino mass eigenvalues are required to explain oscillation phenomena, the Standard Model's three Higgs doublets are insufficient to implement the standard seesaw mechanism, which integrates this feature with electroweak symmetry breaking. In this work, we explore a framework where the majority of the atmospheric neutrino mass splitting arises from radiative corrections. We show that extending the Standard Model with two Higgs doublets, three right-handed neutrinos, and a real scalar sector—encompassing both even and odd parity components—generates a contribution to $\Delta m^{2}_{31}$ comparable to the observed value. This setup offers a solution to the $\mu$-error anomaly and provides a dark matter candidate that

Our analysis directly contrasts these findings with the commonly applied $t_{2g}$-only or $e_g$-only models, selected based on electronic filling. Covering all possible $d$-shell occupancies, we calculate the total magnetic moment, spin, individual orbital occupancies, and the effective spin-orbit coupling strength (renormalized by interactions) as functions of bare interaction parameters, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting, with a focus on regimes relevant to 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. Our results indicate that even a weak spin-orbit coupling can be significantly amplified by electron-electron interactions, potentially driving orbital symmetry breaking and altering electron counts in specific orbitals relative to the non-interacting limit—a phenomenon particularly pronounced in 5d materials. These interactions may also induce a spin transition, such as transitioning from high to low spin states, even when the bare spin-orbit coupling is weaker than the spin-interaction terms, likely due to entanglement between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ states via charge transfer. Ultimately, we argue that in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, electron-electron interactions can produce an effectively strong spin-orbit coupling, a critical ingredient for accurately interpreting the intricate magnetic and magnetic-ordering behaviors observed in these materials. Our statements are supported by outcomes derived from exact diagonalization, $t_{2g}$-Hubbard-$U$ model calculations, and intuitive physical reasoning.

Although GANs have proven effective in creating and altering natural images, their use within the medical field remains nascent. By leveraging the CheXpert dataset, we demonstrate that StyleGAN can be trained to produce authentic chest X-rays. Drawing inspiration from the Cyclic Reverse Generator (CRG) framework, we developed an encoder capable of accurately reconstructing X-rays and inverting latent codes for various challenges identified in prior research. Our primary objective was enabling the modification of X-ray images for specific disease representations. Through quantitative analysis and qualitative visualization, we confirmed that our method successfully encoded and inverted latent codes for CrVd-GAN, an variant of CRG designed with value layers to facilitate value-conditioned generation. Consequently, we achieved accurate genetic modifications of latent codes to simulate the presence or absence of pneumonia and valvular heart disease. This study proves the feasibility of using CRVd-GAN for disease-aware editing of chest X-rays and suggests potential for applying this technique to other modalities and conditions. Future work will focus on enhancing image quality, expanding disease coverage, and improving the model's scale.

The Current Diagnostic Oncogenes list (CDO) offers a structured repository of oncogenes currently druggable by small molecule inhibitors. It compiles genes with standing recommendations from major clinical guidelines (NCCN, ESMO) for sequencing in cancer patients, which have been validated in public databases like ClinVar. Each gene profile includes a summary, links to external resources, counts of valid pathogenic variants, and details on database entries containing these variants. While existing public repositories store germline and somatic variants, no current solution efficiently aggregates data to highlight druggable oncogenes or facilitates the simultaneous examination of numerous variants within a clinical context. The proposed list aims to support the rapid diagnosis and management of patients with germline predisposition to cancer and those with somatic mutations, offering a solution implemented at multiple Portuguese health institutions. This list A-Z collection of profiles is provided as an Excel file and can be further customized for specific clinical needs. The VOncoGenes project address is listed at https://hmatol.ipatimup.pt/VOncogenes.

Complex geometries usually necessitate unstructured mesh discretization, making direct potential evaluation via quadrature computationally expensive. This paper introduces a straightforward, high-order algorithm for calculating Newtonian potentials by leveraging Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary integrals, which are then processed using the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the time required for traditionally costly near-field and self-interaction calculations on unstructured meshes becomes comparable to that of far-field interactions computed via the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). A central component of this algorithm is the high-order 2-D monomial approximation of functions over mesh elements; although often viewed as numerically unstable due to ill-conditioned associated integrals, it is stabilized here through the use of an orthogonal basis derived from the mesh's symmetry group. Although the algorithm was developed with charged particle simulations in mind—where particles are particles of fixed radius—it remains applicable to any simulation involving particles with extended support. Numerical tests confirm the algorithm's accuracy and efficiency. This work provides open-source software, available at https://github.com/bsingh/NewtonianPotential, which implements the method for both Newtonian gravity and electrostatics. The code supports particle simulations where particles have finite size and has been utilized to solve Poisson's equation for charge distributions.

Introduction

Calculating Newtonian potentials for particles with finite extent or sources governed by partial differential equations (such as charge or mass distributions) is a fundamental task in physics and engineering simulations. For unstructured meshes, these calculations can be computationally expensive.
